text: Most organizations' pipeline standards start life as a document — every service pipeline must run a dependency scan, every production deploy needs two approvals. This lesson is about why that document stops working as the org grows, and how to make a required standard structurally unskippable instead of something teams are just supposed to remember.

A policy page works fine for the five teams who read it carefully the week it was written. It does not work for team number two hundred and twelve, hired eighteen months later, who has never seen it and has no reason to go looking. The fix isn't a better document — it's moving the requirement out of prose and into the shared template every team's pipeline already depends on, so they get it the moment they call it.

Putting a step inside the template is a strong default, but it's not airtight on its own — a determined team can still route around it. Closing that gap means wiring the job's name into branch protection's required status checks, so the platform itself refuses to merge a pull request until that specific job reports success, regardless of whether anyone remembered the policy existed.

A standard with zero exceptions tends to get quietly routed around, so a shared template should expose a narrow, visible escape hatch for genuine cases — a legacy repo mid-migration, a library with nothing to scan yet. The skip is possible, but it requires a reason string that shows up in the workflow run and in dashboards, which is nothing like silently never adding the step in the first place.

There's an opposite failure mode worth naming directly: routing every pipeline change through one central platform-team review, for every team, on every change. That protects consistency, but it turns the platform team into a queue that two hundred teams wait behind. The standard itself should be enforced automatically; human review should be reserved for changes to the template itself, not for every repo calling an already-approved template with already-approved inputs.

Get the enforcement structural and the override visible, and a standard survives organizational growth instead of decaying into a document nobody reads. Next lesson turns to the companion problem — once the template itself needs to change, how do you roll that change out across hundreds of repos without breaking all of them at once.
